frameworks.name: Three-Step Super Influencer Process
frameworks.definition: A three-step structured approach to leveraging influencer partnerships: (1) pick the right influencer using audience-size comparison, (2) get them to respond using verification, a magic message, and the Rule of 100, (3) close the deal using Proof-Promise-Plan-Offer preparation.

frameworks.name: Proof-Promise-Plan-Offer Presentation
frameworks.definition: A four-part influencer pitch structure: Promise (the upside they will receive), Proof (evidence via case studies or comparable stats), Plan (next steps and expected effort from each party), Offer (economics structured so the influencer clearly gets the better side of the deal).

frameworks.name: Influencer Outreach Circle Method
frameworks.definition: A layered outreach sequence for identifying and reaching influencers: (1) influencers known personally, (2) second-degree introductions from own network, (3) influencers followed or heard of via multi-channel direct outreach, (4) formal agent or website contact channels.

frameworks.name: Audience-Size Partnership Model
frameworks.definition: A decision rule for structuring influencer partnerships: if your brand's audience is larger than the influencer's, have them promote your brand; if their audience is larger, deliver under their brand. The relative size of audiences determines who promotes and who delivers.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that partnering with a single high-reach influencer (a super influencer) is the highest-ROI single move a business can make because it compresses years of audience-building into weeks, reaching millions of potential buyers for free as long as the product margin exceeds its cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Product gross margin exceeds cost of goods
Super influencer has genuine audience alignment with product category
claims.mechanism: The influencer's audience is already aggregated trust; the business skips the years of audience accumulation and immediately converts pre-existing trust into sales, with no paid acquisition cost on the influencer's traffic.
bounded_by: Requires giving up a portion of economics or ownership to the influencer
Speed advantage disappears if product-market fit is fundamentally absent

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that traditional advertising is declining in cost-efficiency relative to social media and influencer marketing: internet content has more total viewers than television, more podcast listeners than radio listeners, and this audience is larger, cheaper to reach, and converts at higher rates simultaneously.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to consumer goods and B2C products with broad appeal
claims.mechanism: Distribution cost of digital content approaches zero and social platforms surface content algorithmically to interested audiences, reducing CPM while increasing relevance-match compared to broadcast advertising.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the choice between promoting your existing brand through an influencer versus delivering under the influencer's brand is determined solely by whose audience is larger: if the business brand has more reach than the influencer, have the influencer promote the brand; if the influencer has more reach, build and deliver a product branded for them. Nike's Air Jordan line (Nike brand larger than rookie Jordan, so Jordan promoted Nike's specific line) and Congo/Prime (Logan Paul's audience larger than Congo, so Congo delivered under Paul's brand) illustrate both poles.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Partnership is between a product/delivery company and a content creator or athlete
claims.mechanism: Larger audience controls brand association; the party with smaller reach gains more by attaching to the larger brand than by preserving their own name.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that many large influencers (including A-list celebrities) are accessible for partnership for far less money than most business owners assume, citing that superstars can be contracted for a few hundred thousand dollars per year; the actual barrier is outreach execution, not budget.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business owner already has operating infrastructure to deliver on the partnership
Partnership is performance-linked (royalty or revenue share) rather than flat celebrity endorsement
claims.mechanism: Influencers with large audiences but without business operations need delivery partners; the scarcity of qualified delivery partners relative to the volume of influencers reduces the effective cost of access.

numbers.axis: annual cost to secure a super influencer partnership

anchors.value: a few hundred thousand dollars per year for superstars

bounded_by: Does not apply to flat brand endorsement deals with large CPG brands which command higher fees
Assumes performance-aligned deal structure, not guaranteed upfront payment

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that getting a platform verification badge (paying roughly $10/month for a blue check) produces 5 to 10 times higher response rates when cold-messaging influencers on social platforms, making it one of the highest-ROI investments per dollar in outreach.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Outreach is via social platform DMs (Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok)
Influencer receives high message volume making credibility signals decisive
claims.mechanism: A verified profile signals legitimacy and filters out spam at first glance; influencers screen by profile trust before reading message content, so an unverified sender never gets message content evaluated.

numbers.axis: response rate multiplier from platform verification badge

bounded_by: Effect attenuates if the verified profile has no posts or irrelevant content (verification alone is insufficient)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that sending 100 outreach messages per day across multiple platforms is the correct activity target when pursuing influencer partnerships, because despite high apparent competition, actual action-takers are typically only 5% of stated interest; this makes the odds favorable for anyone who executes consistently.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Outreach is personalized, not copy-pasted mass blast
Sender has a verified, professional-looking profile
claims.mechanism: Because most people express interest but do not follow through, the pool of actual competitors in any outreach campaign is roughly 5% of the nominal pool; consistent high-volume outreach by the minority who execute creates statistically reliable response volumes.

numbers.axis: ratio of stated interest to actual submission/action in competitive outreach contexts

anchors.region: stated interest (e.g., job applicants, DM campaign responders)

bounded_by: Volume without personalization reduces response quality to near zero
Platform daily message caps may require splitting across multiple platforms to reach 100

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that reaching out to an influencer on a platform where they have a small following (e.g., LinkedIn) rather than where they have millions of followers (e.g., Instagram) dramatically increases the probability of standing out and receiving a reply, because the inbox on the smaller platform has fewer competing messages.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Influencer actively monitors multiple platforms
claims.mechanism: Inbox scarcity drives response probability: a message in an inbox of 10 faces far less competition for attention than the same message in an inbox of 1,000, even if total reach on the smaller platform is lower.

numbers.axis: number of competing messages in DM inbox by platform

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the single most persuasive proof of future work ethic to a prospective influencer partner is doing extensive preparation work before the first meeting, specifically because influencers' primary concern is whether the business partner will work hard on their behalf; and the best signal of future effort is demonstrated past effort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business owner is seeking a partnership with an influencer who has more audience than the business
No prior relationship or track record with the influencer exists
claims.mechanism: Pre-meeting effort (mock-ups, financial projections, multiple presentation versions) is costly to fake; influencers interpret visible effort as a reliable signal of the partner's future work intensity because the signaling cost is real.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business owner with no track record can still close a super influencer deal by using preparation work from pitches to other influencers (even failed pitches) as portfolio evidence of professionalism, because consistent quality of presentation across multiple influencers signals sustained effort independent of any single successful outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business owner has prepared detailed presentations for at least one other influencer, even if that pitch was rejected
claims.mechanism: Seeing polished preparation materials for multiple named influencers signals a high professional standard; the influencer infers that if this quality was applied to competitors, it will be applied to them, which substitutes for a track record of completed deals.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a smaller, newer business owner should sell the advantages of their size (personal attention, owner mentality, flexibility, cell-phone access) as directly superior to the generic account-rep treatment from market leaders, rather than apologizing for lack of scale; conversely, a market leader should sell track record, infrastructure, and brand-association value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Pitch is to an influencer who is evaluating multiple potential business partners
The business is either clearly a market leader or clearly a newer entrant; not mid-market
claims.mechanism: Influencers evaluate partnerships on two criteria: will the partner care about my audience and brand, and can the partner handle the scale if this succeeds. Small operators win on the first criterion; large operators win on the second. Selling into the criterion you actually win prevents direct comparison on criteria where you lose.
bounded_by: Mid-market businesses that are neither clear underdog nor clear leader have no obvious positional argument and must choose which angle fits best

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that offering to help a mid-sized influencer grow their audience and content output (rather than offering only cash economics) is often more effective than a pure revenue-share offer, because influencers below a certain scale prioritize audience growth over marginal income.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Influencer is in a growth phase (not yet a mega-influencer with maxed-out monetization)
Business partner has content production resources (editors, camera operators, distribution expertise) to offer
claims.mechanism: For an influencer whose income is not yet constrained by audience size, the bottleneck is audience growth rather than monetization; offering production resources that accelerate audience growth addresses their primary constraint and creates shared upside because a larger influencer audience also increases the business partner's revenue.
bounded_by: Does not apply to mega-influencers who are already audience-saturated and income-constrained only by deal quality

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that a gift to an influencer is more effective when it is deeply personalized and clearly required significant time and thought to create, rather than expensive but generic, because the time-cost of the gift signals the same future work ethic that influencers are trying to evaluate in a business partner.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Gift is delivered before the first formal meeting as an outreach step
claims.mechanism: A personalized gift (custom art incorporating the influencer's quotes, branded items with the influencer's logo rather than the sender's) demonstrates that the sender researched the influencer deeply and invested irreversible effort; this mirrors the future effort the influencer wants from a business partner.
bounded_by: Does not work if the gift is expensive but generic (e.g., standard luxury brand items) — those signal money, not attention

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that building a paid online community is a near-universal product structure that fits any influencer because audiences follow influencers specifically to get more access to them; a paid community simply puts the highest-access tier behind a paywall while keeping public content free.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Influencer has an existing engaged following who desire more direct access
Influencer is willing to create exclusive content or interaction within the community
claims.mechanism: Audience willingness to pay is anchored to desire for access; public content creates demand for access and the paid community monetizes the top-desire segment without cannibalizing the free-audience growth flywheel.
bounded_by: Does not work if the influencer's audience is primarily passive consumers rather than engaged fans who want direct interaction

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that putting branded promotional materials with the influencer's logo (not the business owner's logo) on gifts and products dramatically increases the likelihood the influencer will use and display the item, creating repeated positive association between the influencer and the business owner in the influencer's mind.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Gift or product is designed for personal use by the influencer, not for sale
claims.mechanism: Items branded for the influencer rather than the sender serve the influencer's self-presentation interest; items branded for the sender serve the sender's interest. The influencer will display and use the former and set aside the latter, creating or failing to create the positive association the sender intended.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that sharing (resharing stories of) an influencer's existing content on your own social channels is one of the easiest and most effective ways to build initial affinity with that influencer before reaching out, because influencers can see cumulative share counts and interpret repeated shares as evidence of genuine audience alignment and as a form of value already delivered.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Outreach target uses a platform where story reshares are visible to the original poster (e.g., Instagram)
claims.mechanism: Influencers see an accumulated reshare count in their DM history before reading any message; a high reshare count creates a perceived debt or affinity that positively biases the influencer's prior toward the sender before any direct message is read.

examples.text: Nike's 1984 Air Jordan deal illustrates the value of concentrating an influencer budget on a single super influencer. Nike had been spending its basketball budget across five to ten second-tier players and losing the best athletes to Adidas and Converse. Phil Knight's partnership manager insisted they put the entire basketball sponsorship budget into one rookie, Michael Jordan. Because Nike needed Jordan more than Jordan needed Nike, they gave him the largest player deal ever signed at that time. Nike had hoped for $2 million in basketball shoe sales in the first year; they achieved $122 million and built a brand that remained dominant decades later. The lesson Hormozi draws: concentrating resources on the single best-fit influencer dramatically outperforms spreading the same budget across many smaller ones.

Congo (the beverage manufacturer behind Prime and two other brands each doing ~$500M/year in sales) illustrates the deliver-under-the-influencer's-brand model. Congo had no consumer brand recognition, but Logan Paul had massive audience reach. Congo concluded that Logan Paul's audience was larger than their brand's audience, so rather than having Paul promote a Congo product, they created a drink branded entirely around Paul (Prime) and handled all manufacturing and distribution themselves. Within roughly two years, Prime surpassed Powerade (a 36-year-old brand) in sales volume, validating the model of delivering under a super influencer's brand when the influencer's reach exceeds the business's reach.

A Mosey Media hiring contest illustrates the low real-competition threshold in outreach. Hormozi posted one piece of content offering editor roles and received 1,200 expressions of interest. He then sent all 1,200 an identical raw video file and gave them 48 hours to submit an edit. Only 60 of the 1,200 (5%) actually submitted. This pattern — roughly 1-in-20 people who express interest taking action — recurs across job applications, partnership outreach, and social contexts. The implication: anyone who consistently executes faces roughly 20x lower effective competition than the stated interest pool suggests.

Manx and Fahad, two UK entrepreneurs in their early 20s with no audience and no following, used the super influencer process to generate $44,000/month in recurring revenue within 30 days. They identified Eddie Abue, a former UK pro bodybuilder with 50,000 Instagram followers at the time. They reached out via DM exactly as Hormozi described (personalizing the message, promising he would be their only partner), pitched him by emphasizing they would grow his following (his primary motivation rather than money), and offered to handle all content production, editing, story posting, CTAs, and community management. Abue would only make content. They branded the community as the Abue Crew (around him, not them), launched it, and hit $44K MRR in month one. Hormozi notes this places them in the top 1% of US earners and that they succeeded specifically by giving up the upside of brand ownership in exchange for the compressive time benefit of his pre-built audience.

Tony Robbins and Dean Graziosi, who run a large business education portfolio, partnered with Matthew McConaughey to launch the Art of Living event. The product was branded around McConaughey's identity and they handled all operational delivery. The event registered over 2 million people and had nearly 500,000 attend live and over 1 million total viewers — larger than anything Robbins and Graziosi had achieved through their own channels. Hormozi uses this as an example of an established large business using a single super influencer to achieve distribution that years of their own list-building had not matched.

Hormozi describes receiving a custom modern-art piece as a memorable gift example. An artist sent him a full-size canvas with an ace-of-spades background (referencing Hormozi's Las Vegas headquarters) with graffiti-style renditions of quotes that had impacted the artist's life. Hormozi found the gift exceptional because it was clearly time-intensive to produce and deeply researched (tied to his location, his public quotes). He contrasts this with generic branded merchandise: the artist's gift made Hormozi think of the sender every time he saw it; a generic item with the sender's logo would simply be stored.

practices.text: Begin influencer outreach by contacting people you already know personally before attempting cold outreach; even a small mutual follower count or prior interaction materially increases response probability.
When asking your network for influencer introductions, explicitly offer to pay a referral bounty for introductions that convert into partnerships, and state the dollar amount upfront.

Set your social media bio to clearly state that you partner with influencers and describe what type of partnership you are seeking, so any influencer who views your profile understands your intent immediately.

Prepare mock-ups of what the influencer's brand would look like on your product (or of the product you would create for them) before the first meeting; bring physical samples or demos if a tangible product is involved.

Structure influencer partnership economics so the influencer visibly gets the better side of the deal; make your side of the obligations larger and more costly so the influencer feels they are receiving outsized value relative to their effort.

If budget is tight, offer to fly out and meet the influencer in person at your own expense; frame the travel as incidental ("I'm out that way all the time") to avoid making them feel they are inconveniencing you.

Reach out to the same influencer across every platform simultaneously (Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, email, direct mail); the platform where they have fewer followers gives the highest inbox-signal-to-noise ratio and the best chance of standing out.

Prepare financial projections for the influencer before the pitch: estimate their current follower count, post frequency, assumed reach-per-post, assumed 1% click-to-buyer conversion, and project a 12-month revenue outcome to show you actually did the math.
